# Projection and MIP Techniques

Also called: MIP (Maximum Intensity Projection)

## Overview
Projection and MIP Techniques are a family of image-order volume rendering methods that replace the standard front-to-back alpha compositing of [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) with order-independent aggregation functions (maximum, minimum, or summation) along each viewing ray. Unlike standard ray casting which preserves depth cues through opacity accumulation, these techniques discard spatial depth information to emphasize specific intensity ranges, making them distinct from [Direct Volume Rendering](1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) and [Neural volume rendering](1576-neural-volume-rendering.md).

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the ray generation, discretization, and sampling infrastructure defined in the parent [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md). The key deviation lies in the **Compositing** stage. Instead of integrating radiative energy using the over operator, these methods maintain a single scalar accumulator per pixel that is updated via a commutative aggregation function $A$ for each sample $s_i$ along the ray segment $[t_{start}, t_{end}]$:

$$
Acc_{i} = A(Acc_{i-1}, s_i)
$$

where $Acc_0$ is initialized to the identity element of the aggregation function (e.g., $-\infty$ for maximum, $0$ for summation). Because the aggregation is commutative and associative, the result is independent of the sampling order, enabling parallelization and early termination strategies that are not applicable to the non-commutative alpha blending of standard ray casting. The final pixel color is derived by applying a transfer function $T$ to the final accumulated scalar value $Acc_{final}$, rather than blending a sequence of colors.

## Subtopics

### [Maximum Intensity Projection](902-maximum-intensity-projection.md)
Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) selects the voxel with the highest scalar intensity along each ray. It is chosen when visualizing high-density structures (e.g., contrast-enhanced vessels in CT angiography) where the brightest voxels represent the anatomy of interest. It discards all intermediate and lower-intensity data, providing high contrast for bright structures but losing depth cues.

### [Forward Projection (aTx)](1492-forward-projection-atx.md)
Forward projection (X-ray projection) sums all scalar values along the ray path, mimicking the physics of radiographic attenuation. It is chosen when generating 2D projection images that represent total density or attenuation, such as in digital subtraction angiography or bone density assessment. Unlike MIP, it is sensitive to the total mass along the ray, making it difficult to distinguish between a single large object and multiple small objects.

### [Minimum Intensity Projection](5299-minimum-intensity-projection.md)
Minimum Intensity Projection (MinIP) identifies the voxel with the lowest scalar intensity along each ray. It is chosen for visualizing low-intensity structures, such as air-filled vessels or lungs, which are often obscured by higher-intensity tissue in standard rendering. It provides high contrast for dark features but similarly discards depth information.

### [Projection](7205-projection.md)
Projection refers to the direct summation of voxel values along a specific axis (typically parallel to the grid axes) without perspective ray traversal. It differs from ray-based methods by using simple array summation, making it computationally trivial and highly parallelizable. It is used for quick previews or when the viewing direction is strictly aligned with the data axes.

### Projected Slabs Approximation
An algorithm that approximates perspective volume rendering using parallel projected slabs to enable acceleration on hardware designed for parallel projection, with analytical error bounds [S2, unofficial]. The method involves approximating perspective projection using parallel projected slabs, performing an analytical study of maximum and average error, and improving the basic algorithm based on error analysis to bound global maximum error while increasing frame rate [S2, unofficial].

### Perspective Approximation via Orthogonal Slices
An approximation for perspective volume rendering that uses view-orthogonal slices instead of concentric spherical shells, which are expensive to generate [S3]. The only difference from exact ray casting is that the distances of sample positions along a ray depend on the ray's orientation [S3]. The pitfall is that exact perspective ray casting produces associated sample positions forming concentric spherical shells, not planes, and generating these shells is expensive [S3].

## Background
MIP was introduced as a standard technique for visualizing angiographic data, where the high attenuation of contrast agents makes vessels stand out against background tissue [S1, unofficial]. The term "MIP_Mode" appears in early GPU raycasting implementations to distinguish this aggregation mode from standard alpha blending [S1, unofficial]. Forward projection is rooted in the physics of X-ray imaging, where the detector records the line integral of attenuation coefficients. The projection family leverages the commutative nature of addition to simplify rendering pipelines, often used in pre-processing or for specific axis-aligned views.
